--- title: "[Graph.to_directed()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Convert the graph to a directed graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L31999-L32085){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.to_directed() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Convert to directed](/assets/graphs/to-directed.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="An undirected path A, B, C, D with three plain edges. After to_directed(), each undirected edge has become a pair of accent arrows, one in each direction, so the three edges become six." width="100%"} Creates a new graph with the same nodes but directed edges. If the graph is already directed, returns a new copy. For undirected graphs, creates both directions (u->v and v->u) for each edge. Representing each undirected edge as a pair of opposite arcs keeps reachability and shortest-path distances exactly as they were, while letting you treat the two directions separately afterwards. Typical reasons to convert: - running an algorithm that only accepts directed graphs - starting from a symmetric network and then removing or reweighting one direction (e.g., turning a two-way street into a one-way street) - combining the graph with a directed graph in set operations such as `union()` or `compose()`, which require matching directedness Node IDs, labels, and node attributes are carried over unchanged. Both arcs created from an undirected edge get that edge's weight and attributes, so an undirected graph with `m` edges becomes a directed graph with `2m` edges. The arc in each edge's stored direction keeps the edge's ID; the reverse arcs are new edges with fresh IDs, listed after all the originals. The original graph is not modified. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new directed Graph with the same nodes. Edges are bidirectional pairs if the original was undirected, or unchanged copies if it was already directed. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Converting a small undirected path gives a directed graph: ::: {#2765c597 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec undirected = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) directed = undirected.to_directed() directed.is_directed() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Each undirected edge becomes two directed edges, one for each direction: ::: {#f1f377df .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} directed.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 4 ``` ::: ::: This is useful for preparing an undirected network for directional analysis, such as comparing flow in each direction along a road. Each arc keeps the original road's weight: ::: {#57f80006 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} roads = ec.Graph(directed=False) roads.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) roads.add_edges([("A", "B", 5), ("B", "C", 3)]) traffic = roads.to_directed() traffic.get_edge_df() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
shape: (4, 5)
idsourcetargetrelweight

``` ::: ::: It's also the standard way to prepare an undirected graph for algorithms that only operate on directed graphs, like cycle enumeration. Note that each undirected edge now forms a two-node cycle of its own: ::: {#bf409b2f .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(directed=False) g.add_nodes(["X", "Y", "Z"]) g.add_edges([("X", "Y"), ("Y", "Z")]) g_dir = g.to_directed() g_dir.get_cycles() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` [[1, 2], [3, 2]] ``` ::: :::
